title_original: Giada Ripa, Japan and the Silkworms
excerpt_original: The Italian photographer set out for Yokohama on the trail of her forebear and of Felice Beato, a pioneer of 19th-century war photography. With a large-format camera, she takes up his protocol, the full-length pose, the tool of the trade, the plain backdrop, to assemble a…

blocks.text: In the attic of a family house in Piedmont, Italy, Giada Ripa unearths an album signed by Felice Beato. “I came across […] fifty-three hand-coloured albumen prints […] all in pristine condition,” she recalls. An unpublished travel manuscript soon surfaces as well, and the photographer resolves to retrace the journey, “with the same slow, deliberate gaze.”

The album’s maker, Felice Beato, had covered the wars in Crimea, India and China before settling in Yokohama, at a time when the shogun admitted foreigners only on diplomatic missions. A Venetian turned British subject, he hand-tinted his albumen prints with a brush and composed plates of native types: grooms, Buddhist monks, wrestlers. In him Giada Ripa sees “the first visual narrator of 1860s Japanese society.”

The manuscript, for its part, comes from an ancestor of the photographer, Mathilde Ruinart de Brimont, a painter and muse to several intellectuals, who landed in Yokohama in 1867 beside her husband, Vittorio Sallier de La Tour, a gambler frowned upon by her family and minister plenipotentiary of the Kingdom of Italy to the Empire of Japan. Their mission was as much agronomy as diplomacy: the couple had come, the photographer reports, to seek “new silkworm varieties to export to Italy.” Pébrine, the parasite then ravaging Europe’s silkworm nurseries, had devastated the continent’s silk, and only the merchants of Yokohama still held healthy seed.

Between the painter and the Venetian, a friendship took hold. In 1869 the Italian delegation pushed inland toward the Maebashi region, the heart of Japanese silk, on the first foreign expedition into the country’s interior. There the young woman sketched peasant women in pencil, children on their backs, the low islands offshore, while an unnamed photographer captured the caravan’s return outside an inn. On leaving Japan she took Felice Beato’s album home, which would sleep for more than a century in the attic.

First shown at the Kyotographie festival in Kyoto in 2017, the project unfolds in two movements. Giada Ripa first returns to Felice Beato’s vantage points, shooting on film, in his patient, documentary manner. “I followed the light through Yokohama and beyond,” she writes. Where the Venetian had framed the bell tower of a Buddhist temple, she photographs one in Nagasaki, a man in black at the foot of the bell, his hand on the rope from the beam. Farther on, the Hiroshima dome is mirrored in the still waters of the Motoyasu, and at night the avenues of Yokohama dissolve into streaks of headlights beneath an expressway. Her raw color and broad yellow foldouts crack against the sepias of 1868.

blocks.text: In a Tokyo studio, Giada Ripa then summons the bodies of today: a dominatrix, a drag queen crowned with plush white tigers, devotees of Lolita fashion, a near-naked tattoo artist with her machine in hand, a music producer whose guitar is a giant Pocky box. All pose with the gravity Felice Beato reserved for his sitters of old, yet each here has composed a persona of their own. “Their portraits, and our exchanges, form a living archive of contemporary Japan, in dialogue with its past,” the photographer sums up.

Reproduced on thin rice paper, Felice Beato’s prints face Giada Ripa’s modern portraits. His 1868 fishmonger squares off against Toshio Awatake, a wholesaler at Tsukiji market, a scarlet fish wedged against his apron. For the portrait of Kanshin Mochida, head priest of Honkyuji temple, she keeps the Venetian’s caption and merely tips it from plural to singular: “This priest is of the Nichiren-shu sect, an order of about six hundred years standing.” Then she slips into her own frames, a tiny figure in an indigo kimono among the ferns of the Miyagino hot springs, a self-portrait dedicated to Mathilde Ruinart.

The book closes on a wink. Of all these images of the East taken by Westerners, the one Giada Ripa keeps for her cover is the only one drawn by a Japanese hand, which stayed anonymous: the count and his wife entering the country’s interior, ringed by officials. Ever since Felice Beato, the West has gazed at Japan; this time it is Japan that gazes back at us.
